16.8.5.2 Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution Reactions

16.8.5.2.1 General Introduction

Reaction in which hydrogen atom of the aromatic ring is replaced by an electrophile is called electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction. Benzene ring with its delocalized pi electrons is an electron rich system. It is attacked by electrophiles giving substituted products. A generalized electrophilic substitution reaction is shown below. The catalysts most commonly used are acids.

Mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction involves the following three steps.

Step–1: Formation of an electrophile

Step–2: The electrophile attacks the aromatic ring to produce a non-aromatic carbocation called arenium ion or sigma-complex.

The intermediate arenium ion is resonance stabilized and is a hybrid of the following three structures. This resonance-stabilized carbocation is called a sigma-complex because the electrophile is joined to the benzene ring by a new sigma-bond.

Step–3: The intermediate arenium ion is non-aromatic species and is unstable. It loses a proton to form a stable aromatic substitution product.

The overall reaction is the substitution of a proton by an electrophile on the aromatic ring: electrophilic aromatic substitution.

16.8.5.2.2 Nitration

Benzene reacts with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid at 60°C to form nitrobenzene.

While nitration of toluene in above conditions yield a mixture of isomeric o-,m- and p–nitrotoluene, in unequal proportions. The ortho and para products predominate, while very little meta product is obtained due to ortho/para orienting effect of methyl group (see Section 16.8.5.2.7).

In case of nitration, the electrophile is nitronium ion, produced by reaction of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acid. The electrophile nitronium ion attacks on benzene ring and forms substitution products via arenium ion intermediate (Section 16.8.5.2.1).

However, when halogen is treated with toluene in the presence of ultraviolet light, halogenation occurs at aliphatic side chain (methyl group) to yield successively, benzyl chloride, benzal chloride and benzo trichloride. The reaction follow free radical substitution mechanism (Section 16.3), instead of addition.

Tidbit

The name Benzene hexachloride (BHC) is incorrectly used for 1,2,3,4,5,6–hexachlorocyclohexane. The most important isomer for commercial purposes is the Lindane, which is used in shampoos to kill head lice.

16.8.5.2 Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution Reactions

16.8.5.2.1 General Introduction

Reaction in which hydrogen atom of the aromatic ring is replaced by an electrophile is called electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction. Benzene ring with its delocalized pi electrons is an electron rich system. It is attacked by electrophiles giving substituted products. A generalized electrophilic substitution reaction is shown below. The catalysts most commonly used are acids.

Mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction involves the following three steps.

Step–1: Formation of an electrophile

Step–2: The electrophile attacks the aromatic ring to produce a non-aromatic carbocation called arenium ion or sigma-complex.

The intermediate arenium ion is resonance stabilized and is a hybrid of the following three structures. This resonance-stabilized carbocation is called a sigma-complex because the electrophile is joined to the benzene ring by a new sigma-bond.

Step–3: The intermediate arenium ion is non-aromatic species and is unstable. It loses a proton to form a stable aromatic substitution product.

The overall reaction is the substitution of a proton by an electrophile on the aromatic ring: electrophilic aromatic substitution.

16.8.5.2.2 Nitration

Benzene reacts with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of concentrated sulphuric acid at 60°C to form nitrobenzene.

While nitration of toluene in above conditions yield a mixture of isomeric o-,m- and p–nitrotoluene, in unequal proportions. The ortho and para products predominate, while very little meta product is obtained due to ortho/para orienting effect of methyl group (see Section 16.8.5.2.7).

In case of nitration, the electrophile is nitronium ion, produced by reaction of concentrated nitric and sulfuric acid. The electrophile nitronium ion attacks on benzene ring and forms substitution products via arenium ion intermediate (Section 16.8.5.2.1).
